### 4.1. Absolute irreducibility and regularity

In preparation, we encapsulate a useful property in the following lemma. Its proof applies equally well over any field, and since we refer to it within Proposition 3.5 in the setting of a finite field, we provide a general statement over an arbitrary field $\mathcal{K}$ .

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $\mathcal{K}$ be a field. Let $F\in\mathcal{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be monic in $Y$ and irreducible over $\mathcal{K}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , and denote $\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathcal{K}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/F$ . Then $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is a regular extension of $\mathcal{K}$ , namely:

$$ \overline{\mathcal{K}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathcal{K}, $$

if and only if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is absolutely irreducible, that is, irreducible over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ .

We will apply this directly in the proof of Theorem 4.1. We also note that in the context of Theorem 4.2 over a number field $k$ , if for some $i_{0}\in I$ the condition $\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ holds, then $\overline{k}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=k$ , so that $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is a regular extension of $k$ , and then this lemma shows $F$ must be absolutely irreducible.

#### Proof.

Let $F[Y,\bfX]$ be a polynomial such that $\overline{\mathcal{K}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathcal{K}$ and suppose for a contradiction that it is not absolutely irreducible (so it is reducible over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ ). Denote by $\Omega_{F}$ the Galois closure of $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ over $\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{X})$ and set $L:=\overline{\mathcal{K}}\cap\Omega_{F}$ . Notice that since $\Omega_{F}$ is the Galois closure, $L/\mathcal{K}$ must be Galois and hence $L(\bfX)/\mathcal{K}(\bfX)$ is a Galois extension. Since by assumption $F$ is not absolutely irreducible, we can write

$$ F=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}G_{i}(Y,\bfX)\qquad\text{with each $G_{i}(Y,\mathbf{X})\in L[Y,\mathbf{X}]$,} $$

for some $\ell\geq 2$ , with each $G_{i}$ irreducible over $L(\mathbf{X})$ and monic in $Y$ . Now take $W$ to be one of the roots of $F$ so that $\mathcal{L}_{F}\cong\mathcal{K}(\bfX)[W]$ ; then there exists $i$ such that $G_{i}(W)=0$ . Without loss of generality, we may assume $i=1$ , i.e. the polynomial

$$ G_{1}(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{m}+a_{m-1}Y^{m-1}+\cdots+a_{1}Y+a_{0}, $$

with $a_{i}\in L[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ , is the minimal polynomial of $W$ over $L(\bfX)$ (and additionally observe that $m<\deg_{Y}F$ ). By construction, we have that $G_{1}\not\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{X})[Y]$ , since $F$ is the minimal polynomial of $W$ over $\mathcal{K}(\bfX)$ .

We claim that for every $\sigma\in\Gal(\Omega_{F}/\mathcal{L}_{F})$ , we have $\sigma(a_{i})=a_{i}$ for every $i=1,...,m-1$ . We can see that

$$ \begin{split}0&=\sigma(G_{1}(W,\mathbf{X}))=\sigma(W^{m}+a_{m-1}W^{m-1}+\cdots+a_{1}W+a_{0})\\
&=\sigma(W^{m})+\sigma(a_{m-1})\sigma(W^{m-1})+\cdots+\sigma(a_{1})\sigma(W)+\sigma(a_{0})\\
&=W^{m}+\sigma(a_{m-1})W^{m-1}+\cdots+\sigma(a_{1})W+\sigma(a_{0}),\end{split} $$

where in the third step we have used the fact that $\sigma(W)=W$ since $\sigma\in\Gal(\Omega_{F}/\mathcal{L}_{F})$ . That is to say, we conclude that $W$ is a root of the polynomial

$$ \widetilde{G}_{1}:=Y^{m}+\sigma(a_{m-1})Y^{m-1}+\cdots\sigma(a_{1})Y+\sigma(a_{0}). $$

On the other hand, since $G_{1}$ is the minimal polynomial of $W$ over $L(\bfX)$ , $\deg(\widetilde{G}_{1})=\deg(G_{1})=m$ , and $G_{1},\widetilde{G}_{1}$ are both monic, we must have $G_{1}=\widetilde{G}_{1}$ . Hence, we can conclude $\sigma(a_{i})=a_{i}$ for every $\sigma\in\Gal(\Omega_{F}/\mathcal{L}_{F})$ and every $i\in\{1,...,m-1\}$ .

Since $G_{1}\in L[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ but not in $\mathcal{K}(\bfX)[Y]$ , we can find $i_{0}\in\{1,...,m-1\}$ such that $a_{i_{0}}\in L[\bfX]$ but not in $\mathcal{K}(\bfX)$ . Now write

$$ a_{i_{0}}(\bfX)=\sum_{\mathbf{i}}b_{\mathbf{i}}\bfX^{\mathbf{i}}, $$

where $b_{\mathbf{i}}\in L$ ; furthermore there must exist a multi-index $\mathbf{j}$ such that $b_{\mathbf{j}}\in L\setminus\mathcal{K}$ . On the other hand, from the fact that $\sigma(a_{i_{0}})=a_{i_{0}}$ for every $\sigma\in\Gal(\Omega_{F}/\mathcal{L}_{F})$ , it follows that $\sigma(b_{\mathbf{i}})=b_{\mathbf{i}}$ for every $\sigma\in\Gal(\Omega_{F}/\mathcal{L}_{F})$ and for every $\mathbf{i}$ ; that is $b_{\mathbf{i}}\in\mathcal{L}_{F}$ for every $\mathbf{i}$ . In particular, this implies that $b_{\mathbf{j}}\in L\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}\subset\overline{\mathcal{K}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}$ . Under the hypothesis of the lemma, this says that $b_{\mathbf{j}}\in\mathcal{K}$ , which leads us to our contradiction, as we already established that $b_{\mathbf{j}}\in L\setminus\mathcal{K}$ . This establishes that if $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is a regular extension of $\mathcal{K}$ then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is absolutely irreducible.

To prove the other direction, we will prove the contrapositive: supposing that $\mathcal{K}\subsetneq\overline{\mathcal{K}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}$ , we will show that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not absolutely irreducible. Let $\mathcal{K}\subsetneq\mathcal{K}^{\prime}\subset\overline{\mathcal{K}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}$ be a finite extension of $\mathcal{K}$ ; it follows that $\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq\mathcal{K}^{\prime}(\mathbf{X})\subset\mathcal{L}_{F}$ and $[\mathcal{L}_{F}:\mathcal{K}^{\prime}(\mathbf{X})]<[\mathcal{L}_{F}:\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{X})]=\deg_{Y}F.$ Hence, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ cannot be irreducible over $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}(\mathbf{X})$ (since otherwise we would have that $[\mathcal{L}_{F}:\mathcal{K}^{\prime}(\mathbf{X})]=\deg_{Y}F$ ). Hence, we can find $G,H\in\mathcal{K}^{\prime}(\mathbf{X})[Y]$ such that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=G(Y,\mathbf{X})H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ ; this gives us a factorization of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}$ and hence $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not irreducible over $\overline{\mathcal{K}}$ .

∎

### 4.2. Proof of Theorem 4.1 for $n=1$

(I) is the statement that if an extension $M^{\prime}$ satisfies $k(X_{1})\subseteq M^{\prime}\subseteq k(X_{1})[Y]/(F(Y,X_{1}))=\mathcal{L}_{F}$ and $M^{\prime}=k(X_{1})[Y]/R(Y)$ for some polynomial $R$ independent of $X_{1}$ , then $M^{\prime}=k(X_{1})$ . Any extension of the form $M^{\prime}=k(X_{1})[Y]/R(Y)$ is equivalent to $L^{\prime}(X_{1})$ for some extension $L^{\prime}\supset k$ . Thus (I) is equivalent to the statement that if $L^{\prime}$ is some extension with $k\subset L^{\prime}\subset\overline{k}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}$ , then $L^{\prime}=k$ ; this confirms (I) $\Leftrightarrow$ (II). By Lemma 4.3, (II) $\Leftrightarrow$ (III). Finally, (III) $\Leftrightarrow$ (IV) by Noether’s Lemma 3.3 (ii).

### 4.3. Proof of Theorem 4.2 for $n=2$

We first prove all the relations that have brief, elementary arguments. Then we turn to the final more intricate relation (II) $\Leftrightarrow$ (IV), which we extract as a lemma.

((I) $\Rightarrow$ (II)) By definition, $F$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if and only if $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ . For each ${i_{0}}\in I$ , denote $N_{{i_{0}}}:=(\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F})(X_{{i_{0}}})$ , and observe $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})\subseteq N_{i_{0}}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{F}$ . By construction, $N_{i_{0}}$ is an extension of $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ that is not $n$ -genuine. Now under the hypothesis that $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is strongly $n$ -genuine, if for some ${i_{0}}$ it were true that $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})\subsetneq N_{{i_{0}}}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{F}$ , this would be a contradiction to the definition of a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. Thus for each ${i_{0}}\in I$ , $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})=N_{i_{0}}$ . This implies that for each ${i_{0}}\in I$ , $\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}).$

((II) $\Rightarrow$ (I)) We will prove the contrapositive. Suppose $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine: then there exists some intermediate extension $M^{\prime}$ with $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})\subsetneq M^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{L}_{F}$ , which is not $n$ -genuine. In particular, we can write $M^{\prime}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/R(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J})$ for some polynomial $R$ depending only on $Y$ and $\mathbf{X}_{J}$ for some subset $J\subsetneq I$ . For each ${i_{0}}\in I$ , denote $N_{{i_{0}}}:=(\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L_{F}})(X_{{i_{0}}})$ , as in the previous step. Observe that $M^{\prime}\subset N_{{i_{0}}}$ for some ${i_{0}}$ , and this implies $N_{{i_{0}}}\supsetneq k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ . In turn, this implies $\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}\supsetneq k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}),$ in which $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ .

The next elementary arguments assume we have fixed an index $i_{0}$ .

((III) for $i_{0}$ $\Leftrightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}$ ) The condition (III) for a given index $i_{0}$ is equivalent to the condition (IV) for the index $i_{0}$ by (4.1). Indeed, for each $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{|I^{\prime}|}$ , the property

$$ F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}) \overline{k} \deg F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})=\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}) $$

occurs if and only if $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))\neq 0.$

((III) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (II) for $i_{0}$ ) We will proceed by showing the contrapositive. Assume that $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\subsetneq(\overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F})=:M_{i_{0}}$ , so that in particular $[M_{i_{0}}:k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})]\geq 2$ , which implies $[M_{i_{0}}(X_{i_{0}}):k(\mathbf{X}_{I})]\geq 2$ . We want to establish that for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ , we have that $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $\overline{k}.$ First, we observe that $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $M_{i_{0}}(X_{i_{0}})$ . This follows from the fact that $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},X_{I^{\prime}})$ is irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ and so $\deg_{Y}F=[\mathcal{L}_{F}:k(\mathbf{X}_{I})]$ , while on the other hand $[\mathcal{L}_{F}:k(\mathbf{X}_{I})]=[\mathcal{L}_{F}:M_{i_{0}}(X_{i_{0}})][M_{i_{0}}(X_{i_{0}}):k(\mathbf{X}_{I})]$ , in which the last factor is $\geq 2$ . From this we conclude that $[\mathcal{L}_{F}:M_{i_{0}}(X_{i_{0}})]<\deg_{Y}F$ , and hence $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $M_{i_{0}}(X_{i_{0}})$ as claimed.

Finally, for any choice of $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ , let $M_{i_{0},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}}$ denote the specialization of the field $M_{i_{0}}$ at the choice $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ . Consequently, we have that for any choice of $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in k^{n-1}$ , $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $M_{i_{0},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}}$ . Since $M_{i_{0},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}}\subset\overline{k}$ , this completes the claim.

To complete the proof of the theorem, it suffices to show that (II) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}$ . This we will derive in Lemma 4.5, via the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.4.

Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension. Let $I$ be an index set of cardinality $n\geq 2$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ be irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ and define $\mathcal{L}_{F}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/F$ . Suppose that for some $i_{0}\in I$ and $I^{\prime}:=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ ,

$$ \overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}), $$

that is to say, $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ . Then, there exists a nonempty open set $V\subset k^{n-1}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in V$ ,

$$ \overline{k}\cap(k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\bfx_{I^{\prime}}))=k, $$

that is to say, $k$ is integrally closed in $k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\bfx_{I^{\prime}})$ .

#### Proof.

Let $i_{0}$ be fixed as in the hypothesis. Consider $W=\text{Spec}\left(k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]/F\right)$ and the morphism $f$ induced by the inclusion $k[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]\subset k[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]/F$ , namely:

$$ f:W\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n-1}. $$

Let $V^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n-1}$ be the set of the $u\in\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n-1}$ such that the fiber

$$ f_{u}:W_{u}\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}_{k(u)}^{n-1} $$

is geometrically integral (i.e. $k(u)$ is integrally closed in $K(W_{u})$ ). (Here we use the standard notation that $k(u)$ is the residue field at $u$ and $K(W_{u})$ is the field of rational functions on $W_{u}$ , following e.g. [Har77, Chapter II, section $3$ , page 89].) By [Gro66, EGA IV part 3, Theorem $9.7.7$ ], the set $V^{\prime}$ is locally constructible. On the other hand, the fiber on the generic point $\eta$ , say $f_{\eta}$ , is geometrically integral; this follows from the hypothesis that $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/F=K(W)$ . Consequently, the generic point $\eta$ lies in $V^{\prime}$ . Hence, since it contains the generic point, $V^{\prime}$ contains an open subset $U^{\prime}$ : indeed, since $V^{\prime}$ is locally constructible we can find an open covering $\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n-1}=\bigcup_{i}V_{i}$ such that for each $i$ , $V_{i}\cap V^{\prime}$ is a constructible set, i.e. it is a finite union of sets of the type $S\cap T^{c}$ for $T,S$ open sets. Since $\eta\in V^{\prime}$ , we can find $i$ such that $\eta\in V_{i}\cap V^{\prime}$ , but then we can find $S,T$ open sets such that $\eta\in S\cap T^{c}$ . On the other hand, since $\{\eta\}$ is dense in $\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n-1}$ , it follows that $T=\emptyset$ . Then it suffices to set $U^{\prime}=S\subset(V_{i}\cap V^{\prime})\subset V^{\prime}$ . Finally, we take $V$ to be the open set $V=U^{\prime}\subseteq k^{n-1}$ ; for every $u\in V$ , which we will denote in terms of coordinates by $u=\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ , we have that $k(u)=k$ is integrally closed in $K(W_{u})=\text{Frac}\left(k[Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}]/F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})\right)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.5 ((II) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}$ ).

Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension. Let $I$ be an index set of cardinality $n\geq 2$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ be irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ and define $\mathcal{L}_{F}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/F$ . Suppose that for some $i_{0}\in I$ and $I^{\prime}:=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ ,

$$ \overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}), $$

that is to say, $k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ . For this index $i_{0}$ , define the polynomial $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ as in (4.1), to detect whether $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Then $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))$ is not identically zero as a polynomial in $\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}$ .

#### Proof.

By Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem (Lemma 2.2), since $F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is irreducible over $k$ , there exists a dense set $U\subset k^{n-1}$ such that

$$ F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})\text{ is irreducible over }k,\forall\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U. $$

On the other hand, expand $F$ as a polynomial in $Y,X_{i_{0}}$ as in (4.2), and consider the polynomial $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))$ as in (4.1). We will use Lemma 4.4 to show that in particular there exists some $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U$ such that $B_{\mathrm{red}}((a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})))\neq 0$ . Assume for contradiction that $B_{\mathrm{red}}=0$ on $U$ . Then $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (or $\deg F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})<\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}F$ ) for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U$ . We first argue that there exists a dense subset $U^{\prime}\subset U$ such that $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U^{\prime}$ . Indeed, if we let $W$ denote the subset of $U$ where $\deg F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})<\deg_{Y,X_{i_{0}}}F$ for $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in W$ , we claim $W$ is nowhere dense, so that $U^{\prime}=U\setminus W$ then is the desired set. Now $W$ is contained in a finite union of sets, each of which is defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial (a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ , that defines the coefficient of a certain monomial in $Y,X_{i_{0}}$ in $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ ), and so $W$ is a proper closed subset of lower dimension, and is nowhere dense.

Now recall that by the construction in (4.3), for each $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U^{\prime}\subset U$ , $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is irreducible over $k$ yet reducible over $\overline{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ ; hence $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ must be reducible over some extension $k^{\prime}$ with $k\subsetneq k^{\prime}\subset\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (with $k^{\prime}$ depending on $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ ). So, for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U^{\prime}$ , $k$ cannot be integrally closed in $k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\bfx_{I^{\prime}})$ since its integral closure will contain $k^{\prime}$ . (Alternatively, apply Lemma 4.3 to see that $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ reducible over $\overline{k}$ implies $k\subsetneq\overline{k}\cap k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\bfx_{I^{\prime}})$ .) On the other hand, by Lemma 4.4, there exists a nonempty open set $V\subset k^{n-1}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in V$ , $k$ is integrally closed in $k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\bfx_{I^{\prime}})$ . Since $U^{\prime}$ is dense and $V$ is open, $U^{\prime}\cap V\neq\emptyset.$ Thus, we get a contradiction: if an element $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}$ exists in $U^{\prime}\cap V$ , $k$ would be both integrally closed and not integrally closed in $k(X_{i_{0}})[Y]/F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\bfx_{I^{\prime}})$ .

Thus the supposition that $B_{\mathrm{red}}=0$ on $U$ must be false. In particular, there exists a choice of $\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}\in U$ such that $B_{\mathrm{red}}((a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})))\neq 0$ , and finally $B_{\mathrm{red}}((a_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})))$ is a polynomial in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ that is not identically zero.

∎

This completes the proof of Theorem 4.2 for $n\geq 2$ .

#### Remark 4.6.

Recall from Definition 1.3 that $F$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if $F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ and monic in $Y$ , and $k[Y](\mathbf{X}_{I})/F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. In [BPW25] we defined a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial $F$ to be an absolutely irreducible polynomial (irreducible over $\overline{k}$ ) that is monic in $Y$ and such that $k[Y](\mathbf{X}_{I})/F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. Notice that if Definition 1.3 holds, then property (II) in Theorem 4.2 holds for any index $i_{0}\in I$ . This implies that $\overline{k}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=k$ , so that by Lemma 4.3, $F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is irreducible over $\overline{k}$ , so that any polynomial that is strongly $n$ -genuine in the sense of Definition 1.3 (and monic in $Y$ ) is strongly $n$ -genuine in the sense of [BPW25].

### 4.4. Natural consequence for strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials

Here we prove the quantitative property that follows from being strongly $n$ -genuine.

#### Theorem 4.7.

Let $n\geq 2$ . Let $k/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{k}$ and $m=[k:\mathbb{Q}]$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{O}_{k}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial of total degree $D$ . Then for all $B\gg 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n-1},\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq B:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$}\}\ll_{m,n,\deg F}B^{n-2}(\log B)^{(n-2)(m-1)}. $$

Also, there exists a finite set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}$ , with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{m,n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , such that for all $\mathfrak{p}\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in k_{\mathfrak{p}}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{k_{\mathfrak{p}}}$}\}\ll_{n,\deg F}|k_{\mathfrak{p}}|^{n-2}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.6.

Theorem 1.6 is simply the special case when $k=\mathbb{Q}$ , $k_{\mathfrak{p}}=\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , so that $|k_{\mathfrak{p}}|=|\mathbb{F}_{p}|=p$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.7.

Since $F$ is strongly $n$ -genuine, by Theorem 4.2 (IV), for each $i_{0}\in I$ and $I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ , the form $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ that detects whether $F(Y,X_{i_{0}},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $\overline{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not identically zero. In particular this is true for $i_{0}=1$ . Thus to prove the first claim, it suffices to observe that by Noether’s Lemma 3.3 (ii) followed by the trivial bound in Lemma 2.3 and then Lemma 2.4,

$$ \displaystyle\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime} \displaystyle\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n-1},\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq B:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$}\} \displaystyle\leq\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}_{k}^{n-1},\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq B:B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))=0\}\ll_{m,n,D}B^{n-2}(\log B)^{(n-2)(m-1)}. $$

For the second claim, we define $\mathcal{E}$ to be the set of all prime ideals that divide the gcd, call it $g$ , of the coefficients of $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ . Note that $g\leq\|B_{\mathrm{red}}\|$ and by Lemma 3.3, $\log\|B_{\mathrm{red}}\|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|$ . Consequently by Lemma 2.4, $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{m,n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ . Then for $\mathfrak{p}\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))$ is not identically zero over $k_{\mathfrak{p}}$ . Thus to prove the second claim, we apply Noether’s Lemma 3.3 (ii) followed by the trivial bound in Lemma 2.3:

$$ \displaystyle\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime} \displaystyle\in k_{\mathfrak{p}}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{k_{\mathfrak{p}}}$}\} \displaystyle\leq\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in k_{\mathfrak{p}}^{n-1}:B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}}))=0\}\leq\deg B_{\mathrm{red}}|k_{\mathfrak{p}}|^{n-2}. $$

Since $B_{\mathrm{red}}\ll_{n,D}1$ , this suffices. ∎

#### Remark 4.8.

As the method of proof showed, Theorem 4.7 (and analogously Theorem 1.6) is still true under the following weaker hypothesis: that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $k(\mathbf{X})$ and that for $i_{0}=1$ and $I^{\prime}=\{2,\ldots,n\}$ ,

$$ \overline{k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=k(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}). $$

For then by Lemma 4.5, the polynomial $B_{\mathrm{red}}(a_{\ell,j}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ that detects whether $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}_{I^{\prime}})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not identically zero, and the above proof can proceed.

## 5. Special case of Theorem 1.2, and reduction to the special case

With the theory of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials in hand, we return to the verification of Theorem 1.2 in a special case (Theorem 1.8). Recall the notation associated to Theorem 1.2, as defined in §3.3. Thus $\Omega_{F}$ is the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $K(\bfX)$ and $L_{F}=\Omega_{F}\cap\overline{K}$ , so that $K(\bfX)\subset L_{F}(\bfX)\subset\Omega_{F}$ . We define $M_{F}(Y,\bfX)\in L_{F}(\bfX)[Y]$ to be the minimal polynomial of $\Omega_{F}$ over $L_{F}(\bfX)$ ; so we may assume that $M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is monic in $Y$ and irreducible over $L_{F}(\mathbf{X})$ , and $\Omega_{F}=L_{F}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/(M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})).$

### 5.1. Verification of Theorem 1.8 for $n=1$

For $n=1$ , if $M_{F}$ is strongly $1$ -genuine then (in the notation of Proposition 3.5 (i)) $B_{\mathrm{red},1}^{M_{F}}\in\mathbb{Z}$ is nonzero, by Theorem 4.1 (I) $\Rightarrow$ (IV). Consequently the hypotheses of Proposition 3.5 are all met, so the remainder of the proof of Theorem 1.2 as in [Coh81, Thm. 2.1] can proceed, verifying the case $n=1$ of Theorem 1.8.

#### Remark 5.1 (Original proof is correct for $n=1$ ).

Cohen’s original proof requires no modification when $n=1$ : in the set-up where $M_{F}(Y,X_{1})$ is the minimal polynomial of $\Omega_{F}$ over $L_{F}$ , $M_{F}$ must be strongly $1$ -genuine. Indeed, it is strongly $1$ -genuine by Theorem 4.1 (II) $\Rightarrow$ (I) since by definition $L_{F}:=\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\cap\Omega_{F}=\overline{L_{F}}\cap\Omega_{F}$ . Thus for $n=1$ , Theorem 1.2 is equivalent to Theorem 1.8.

### 5.2. Verification of Theorem 1.8 for $n\geq 2$

For $n\geq 2$ , suppose that for some $i_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , upon defining $I^{\prime}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ ,

$$ \overline{L_{F}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\Omega_{F}=L_{F}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}), $$

that is to say $L_{F}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $\Omega_{F}$ . Then (in the notation of Proposition 3.5 (ii)) $B_{\mathrm{red},i_{0}}^{M_{F}}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ is not identically zero by Theorem 4.2 (II) for $i_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ (IV) for $i_{0}$ . Moreover, this discussion has proved another special case of Theorem 1.2, in which (5.2) is the condition called (*) in the discussion below Theorem 1.8.

#### Theorem 5.2.

Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a number field with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ have total degree at most $D$ and Galois group $G$ over $K(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . If $n\geq 2$ suppose the additional condition: for some $i_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , upon defining $I^{\prime}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ ,

$$ \overline{L_{F}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}})}\cap\Omega_{F}=L_{F}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}), $$

If $n=1$ , no additional condition is required. Then there exists a constant $c$ depending only on $n,D,K$ such that for all $N\geq 3$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n},\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq N:\text{$G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G$}\}\ll_{n,D,K}\|F\|^{c}N^{n-\frac{1}{2}}\log N. $$

### 5.3. A general notion of $\ell$ -genuine and strongly $\ell$ -genuine polynomials

Before beginning the recovery of Theorem 1.2 in full generality, we need to introduce a generalized notion of $\ell$ -genuine and strongly $\ell$ -genuine polynomials in $Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ , now allowing $1\leq\ell\leq n$ to be considered. (We continue to state the definitions over a number field $k$ , although the elementary considerations of this section apply without change in the case of an arbitrary field.)

#### Definition 5.3 ( $\ell$ -genuine extension).

We say that a finite (nontrivial) extension $M$ of $k(\mathbf{X})=k(X_{1},\dots,X_{n})$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension if for every $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in k[Y,\mathbf{X}]=k[Y,X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]$ such that

$$ M=k(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X})), $$

there is some index set $|I|\geq\ell$ such that $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has nonzero degree in $X_{i}$ for all $i\in I$ . We say that $M$ is a strongly $\ell$ -genuine extension of $k(\mathbf{X})$ if for all subextensions $M^{\prime}$ satisfying

$$ k(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq M^{\prime}\subset M, $$

$M^{\prime}$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension of $k(\mathbf{X})$ .

We will require the following simple observation about strongly $1$ -genuine extensions; this merely applies the reasoning of Remark 5.1 in an $n$ -variable setting.

#### Lemma 5.4.

Let $k$ be a number field and let $\mathcal{L}$ be a nontrivial extension of $k(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . The following are equivalent:

(I) $k=\mathcal{L}\cap\overline{k}$ , or equivalently there is no number field $k^{\prime}$ with $k\subsetneq k^{\prime}\subset(\mathcal{L}\cap\overline{k})$ .

(II) $\mathcal{L}$ is a strongly $1$ -genuine extension of $k(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ .

(III) For any extension $\mathcal{M}$ with $k(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\subsetneq\mathcal{M}\subset\mathcal{L}$ , $\mathcal{M}$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension of $k(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ for some $\ell\geq 1$ .

#### Proof.

An extension $k^{\prime}$ with $k\subsetneq k^{\prime}\subset(\overline{k}\cap\mathcal{L})$ exists if and only if $k(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq k^{\prime}(\mathbf{X})\subset\mathcal{L}$ , if and only if there exists a polynomial $G(Y)$ independent of $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ and with $\deg_{Y}G\geq 2$ , such that $k(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq k(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/G(Y)\subset\mathcal{L}$ , which occurs if and only if $\mathcal{L}$ is not strongly $\ell$ -genuine for any $\ell\geq 1$ . Thus (I) $\Leftrightarrow$ (II). Similarly, (II) $\Leftrightarrow$ (III) since $\mathcal{L}$ is strongly $1$ -genuine if and only if for every polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ such that $k(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq k(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}))\subset\mathcal{L}$ , $\deg_{X_{i}}G\geq 1$ for some $i$ , which is equivalent to (III). ∎

#### Corollary 5.5.

Let $\Omega_{F}$ be the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $K(\bfX)$ , $L_{F}:=\Omega_{F}\cap\overline{K}$ , and $M_{F}(Y,\bfX)\in L_{F}(\bfX)[Y]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\Omega_{F}$ over $L_{F}(\bfX)$ . Then there is no number field extension $L^{\prime}\supsetneq L_{F}$ such that

$$ L_{F}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq L^{\prime}(\mathbf{X})\subset\Omega_{F}=L_{F}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/(M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})). $$

Equivalently $M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $1$ -genuine over $L_{F}$ , and $\Omega_{F}$ is a strongly $1$ -genuine extension of $L_{F}(\mathbf{X})$ , in the sense that every extension $\mathcal{M}$ with $L_{F}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\subsetneq\mathcal{M}\subseteq\Omega_{F}$ is an $\ell$ -genuine extension of $L_{F}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ for some $\ell\geq 1$ .

#### Proof.

For the first claim, by construction, since $L_{F}:=\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F}$ , no number field $L^{\prime}$ with $L_{F}\subsetneq L^{\prime}\subset(\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F})=(\overline{L_{F}}\cap\Omega_{F})$ exists. For the equivalence, we may apply Lemma 5.4. ∎

### 5.4. Reduction of the general case for $n\geq 2$

With Corollary 5.5 in hand, we begin discussing the strategy to recover Theorem 1.2 in full generality by reducing to an application of Theorem 5.2. From now on we need only consider the case $n\geq 2$ . We introduce a notation for a shifted polynomial: for any $\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ define

$$ F_{\bfa}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})=F(Y,X_{1},X_{2}+a_{2}X_{1},...,X_{n}+a_{n}X_{1}). $$

This is a linear transformation, say $F_{\mathbf{a}}(Y,\mathbf{X})=F(Y,\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{X}))$ where $\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}\in\text{GL}_{n}(K)$ has associated matrix

$$ \sigma_{\mathbf{a}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&0&\ldots&0\\
a_{2}&1&\ldots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
a_{n}&0&\ldots&1\end{array}\right). $$

#### Lemma 5.6.

In the notation of Corollary 5.5, for each $\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ , $L_{(F_{\mathbf{a}})}=L_{F}$ . Moreover, $(M_{F})_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X})=M_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , that is to say, the shift of the minimal polynomial is the minimal polynomial of the shift.

#### Proof.

We first prove that for $\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ , $L_{(F_{\mathbf{a}})}=L_{F}$ . Since by definition $L_{F}:=\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F}$ , note that $L_{F}=\cap_{\mathbf{x}\in K^{n}}\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F,\mathbf{x}}$ , where $\Omega_{F,\mathbf{x}}$ is the splitting field of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ . On the other hand, $L_{(F_{\mathbf{a}})}=\cap_{\mathbf{x}\in K^{n}}\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F,\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x})}=\cap_{\mathbf{x}\in\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}(K^{n})}\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F,\mathbf{x}}$ , in which $\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}$ is the linear transformation associated to $\mathbf{a}$ , as defined above. Now, $\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}\in\text{GL}_{n}(K)$ is invertible, so indeed $L_{(F_{\mathbf{a}})}=\cap_{\mathbf{x}\in K^{n}}\overline{K}\cap\Omega_{F,\mathbf{x}}=L_{F},$ and the claim is proved.

For the second claim, we will show that $\Omega_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}=L_{F}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(M_{F})_{\mathbf{a}}(Y,\mathbf{X}).$ Let us write $k:=L_{F}=L_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}$ and $\Omega_{F}=k(\mathbf{X})(\alpha_{1}(\mathbf{X}),\ldots,\alpha_{D}(\mathbf{X}))$ , where $\alpha_{i}(\mathbf{X})$ are algebraic expressions and the roots of $F(Y,\mathbf{X}).$ Then since $\Omega_{F}=k(\mathbf{X})[Y]/M_{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , we know that $\alpha_{i}(X_{1},X_{2}+a_{2}X_{1},...,X_{n}+a_{n}X_{1})\in k(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(M_{F})_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ for each $i$ . Thus, $\Omega_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}\subset k(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(M_{F})_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X}).$ Furthermore, we know that

$$ [\Omega_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}:k(\mathbf{X})]=[\Omega_{F}:k(\mathbf{X})]=[k(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(M_{F})_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X}):k(\mathbf{X})]. $$

Hence $\Omega_{F_{\bfa}}=k(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(M_{F})_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ as desired.

∎

We will transform $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ to produce a shifted polynomial $F_{\mathbf{a}}$ whose corresponding minimal polynomial $M_{F_{\mathbf{a}}}(Y,\mathbf{X})=(M_{F})_{\mathbf{a}}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies the hypothesis (5.2) for $i_{0}=1$ , and moreover $\log\|F_{\mathbf{a}}\|\ll_{n,D,m}\log\|F\|$ , via the following theorem.

#### Theorem 5.7.

Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension and denote $m=\deg(K/\mathbb{Q})$ . Suppose $n\geq 2$ and let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a squarefree polynomial of total degree $D$ and $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ . For any $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ , let $\Omega_{\bfa}$ be the splitting field of $F_{\bfa}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $K(\mathbf{X})$ and define the number field

$$ L:=L_{(F_{\mathbf{a}})}=\Omega_{\bfa}\cap\overline{K}=\Omega_{F}\cap\overline{K}=L_{F}, $$

which is independent of $\mathbf{a}$ by Lemma 5.6. Then there exists some $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ with $\|\bfa\|\ll_{n,D,m}1$ such that

$$ \overline{L(X_{2},...,X_{n})}\cap\Omega_{\mathbf{a}}=L(X_{2},...,X_{n}). $$

We will prove this theorem in §6 and §7. For now, we show why it suffices to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2.

#### Deduction of Theorem 1.2.

In Theorem 1.2, consider the given polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ in $\mathcal{O}_{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of total degree $\leq D$ and Galois group $G$ over $K(\mathbf{X})$ . Fix once and for all a choice of $\bfa\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n-1}$ provided by Theorem 5.7 so that (5.4) holds, and define the shifted polynomial $F_{\bfa}$ as in (5.3). Since $\|\mathbf{a}\|\ll_{n,D,m}1$ , then $\|F_{\mathbf{a}}\|\ll_{n,D,m}\|F\|$ ; this follows from the relation that for any $a\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(a)|\ll_{m}H_{K}(a).$ Similarly, the property $\|\bfa\|\ll_{n,D,m}1$ implies that if $\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq N$ then $\mathbf{x}_{\bfa}:=(x_{1},x_{2}-a_{1}x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}-a_{n}x_{1})$ also satisfies $\|\mathbf{x}_{\bfa}\|\ll_{n,D,m}N$ ; this follows from the triangle inequality after expressing $x_{1},\dots,x_{n}$ in terms of the chosen integral basis for $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ that defines the height $H_{K}(\cdot)$ . (Note the complementary signs of this shift, so that tautologically $F_{\bfa}(Y,x_{\bfa})=F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ for every $\bfa$ .)

For each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n}$ , denote the Galois group of $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ over $K$ by $G(\mathbf{x})$ . Our aim is to show that

$$ \#\{\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq N:G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G\}\ll_{n,D}\|F\|^{c/3}N^{n-1/2}\log N, $$

for some $c$ depending only on $n,D,K$ . Given $\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}^{n}$ , let $G_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{z})$ denote the Galois group of $F_{\mathbf{a}}(Y,\mathbf{z})$ over $K$ . If $G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G$ , then tautologically $G_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x}_{\bfa})\not\simeq G$ . Thus,

$$ \#\{\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq N:G(\mathbf{x})\not\simeq G\}\leq\#\{\|\mathbf{x}_{\bfa}\|\ll_{n,D,m}N:G_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x}_{\bfa})\not\simeq G\}. $$

Because (5.4) holds, Theorem 5.2 applies to $F_{\mathbf{a}}$ , so that for some $c$ (depending on $n,D,K$ ), for all $N\geq 3$ ,

$$ \#\{\|\mathbf{z}\|\ll_{n,D,m}N:G_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{z})\neq G\}\ll_{n,D,K}\|F_{\mathbf{a}}\|^{c}N^{n-1/2}\log N\ll_{n,D,K}\|F\|^{c}N^{n-1/2}\log N, $$

where we have applied $\|F_{\bfa}\|\ll_{n,D,m}\|F\|$ .

∎

Consequently, all that remains to recover Theorem 1.2 is to prove Theorem 5.7. To do so, we first need to characterize the properties of $n$ -genuine polynomials (analogous to Theorem 4.2); we turn to this in the next section.
